title: Cold, Far and Looking Back
paragraphs: Placing a telescope about one and a half million kilometres from Earth may seem an extravagant choice, since anything that goes wrong out there is effectively beyond repair. Yet the James Webb Space Telescope, launched on Christmas Day in two thousand twenty one, was deliberately sent to that distance, where it circles a point known as the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point. At such a location, the combined gravity of the two bodies allows a spacecraft to hold a stable position with very little fuel. That makes reliability the first requirement of the whole design, and it explains the years of testing that came before launch.

The reason for such remoteness lies in the instrument itself. Webb is an infrared observatory, and infrared detection is easily swamped by heat. Keeping the observatory far from Earth helps it avoid the warmth of our planet, so that its sensitive instruments can stay cold. The primary mirror, roughly six and a half metres across, is assembled from eighteen hexagonal segments coated with gold, and these segments act together as a single surface.

Because light travels at a finite speed, the faintest objects Webb detects are also the oldest: their light left home long before Earth existed. Observing them is therefore less like taking a photograph than reading an old letter. Astronomers hope the data will reveal how some of the first galaxies formed, although interpreting such faint signals will demand years of careful analysis. Whatever the results turn out to be, the mission already shows how far careful engineering can extend human sight.
